newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: POST MORTEM ON EX-POLICEMAN FOUND HANGED IN PRISON
A post mortem will be conducted on the body of former policeman Clinton Moller.
The 27-year old was found hanging by a skipping rope in his cell at Sydney's Parklea prison last Saturday.
Moller's mother is seeking an independent inquiry into her son's death.
His lawyer, Ken Madden, says more questions than usual surround Clinton Moller's death.
A coronial inquest will be held later this year.
EMPLOYER ACCESS TO PAEDOPHILE DATABASE PROPOSED
Police will tell employers of the presence of convicted and suspected child sex offenders on thier organisation, if Federal Crime agencies have their way.
The Australian Bureau of Criminal Intelligence will present a plan for such an iniative to Australiasian Police Ministers when they meet in July.

The Australian Bureau of Criminal Intelligence says barriers which prevent the release of information on suspects to third parties must be removed if a national database on paedophiles is to protect children.
The matter was raised at a conference on paedophilia in Sydney.
It was told that as part of the initiative, a national body would be established to screen child sex offenders from employment in which they are likely to interact with children.
KERNOT'S NATIVE TITLE SOLUTION
Democrats Leader, Cheryl Kernot, has suggested a three-pronged solution to the impasse over native title, which avoids extinguishment.
Senator Kernot says the solution could involve codifying the rights of stakeholders, regional agreements and localised case-by-case arrangements.
She was speaking in Queensland's Central West after talks with rural women about the High Court's Wik ruling.
Senator Kernot says the Prime Minister John Howard will want to avoid extinguishing Native Title, but he may have to appease the National Party.
BORE CAPPING PROGRAM COULD HIT PASTORALISTS
The National Farmers' Federation is urging the Federal Government to be cautious about speeding up a program of capping bores in the outback.
A new report by the C-S-I-R-O recommends that most artificial water resources in nature reserves and some pastoral properties should be shut off.
The study found the presence of dams, bores and water channels affected up to a third of native plants and animals which were evolved to survive far from regular water sources.
A capping program is already underway.
But the N-F-F's Harry Bonanno says he's concerned about the proposal to accelerate the process, because of its impact on the pastoral industry.
